title: WAV vs MP3: Which Copy Should You Keep for Editing?
description: Keep the WAV master for editing and make an MP3 copy for sharing when the recipient accepts it.
direct: Keep the WAV you edit from. Export MP3 as a separate delivery copy when you need a smaller file and the recipient accepts MP3.

cards.choice.heading: Choose by next task
cards.choice.body: A larger WAV file can be a useful editing source, while a smaller MP3 is convenient for delivery. The filename alone does not establish recording quality: a WAV made from an MP3 still contains the earlier losses.
sections.explain.heading: Avoid repeated lossy exports
sections.explain.body: If you need to trim or process a recording again, return to the best available source. Repeated MP3 exports can accumulate artifacts. A higher bitrate can reduce audible losses, but it cannot guarantee transparency for every recording or recreate missing frequencies.
sections.practice.heading: A practical archive habit
sections.practice.body: Name the files so that the editable master and delivery copy cannot be confused. Keep both until the recipient has checked the result. This workflow does not promise lossless MP3 output, noise removal or a particular size reduction.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: I received only an MP3. What should I keep?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: Save that MP3 untouched as the best available original. If an editor requires WAV, make a working copy and keep it separate.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: How should I name the two versions?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: Use purpose in the name, such as interview-master.wav and interview-share.mp3. Check the extension and open the attachment before sending it.
